title: Programmatic Access: SDKs, Cloud Shell, Cloud Code, Emulators, and Gemini Cloud Assist
bodyMarkdown:
# Programmatic Access: SDKs, Cloud Shell, Cloud Code, Emulators, and Gemini Cloud Assist

Architects guide teams on how to work with Google Cloud beyond the console: the command-line tools, browser and IDE environments, local emulators, client libraries, and the authentication model that ties them together. The exam checks two habits: choose the **current recommended tool** (for example `gcloud storage` over `gsutil`), and **never reach for a downloaded service account key** when an attached identity or federation exists.

## Command-line tools

| Tool | Use for | Status and notes |
|---|---|---|
| `gcloud` | Managing most Google Cloud resources (compute, IAM, run, container, deploy, and more) | The primary CLI |
| `gcloud storage` | Cloud Storage buckets and objects | Recommended Cloud Storage CLI |
| `gsutil` | Cloud Storage (legacy) | Minimally maintained; still valid in existing scripts |
| `bq` | BigQuery: `bq load`, `bq query`, `bq mk`, `bq extract` | `bq cp` copies tables, not Cloud Storage objects |

The [gsutil documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/gsutil) is blunt: gsutil "is not the recommended CLI for Cloud Storage." It is legacy and minimally maintained, it does not support newer features such as soft delete and managed folders, and `gcloud storage` "require[s] less manual optimization in order to achieve the fastest upload and download rates." After March 2027, gsutil will no longer ship inside the Google Cloud CLI installation package and will be available only as a standalone PyPI install. Existing scripts that use `gsutil -m cp -r` (the `-m` flag runs operations in parallel) remain valid, but new work should use `gcloud storage cp -r gs://source gs://dest`.

Loading data with `bq` follows the [documented pattern](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/loading-data-cloud-storage-json): `bq load --source_format=NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON --autodetect dataset.table gs://bucket/data.json`. Use `--autodetect` instead of supplying a schema file when the schema can be inferred. The distractors on this topic are always invented commands (`gsutil load`, `gcloud bigquery import`) or `bq cp` used on files.

Retries: Cloud Storage's [retry strategy](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy) treats HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx responses and socket timeouts as retryable; the gcloud CLI retries with truncated binary exponential backoff, with a default maximum of 32 retries. Retrying is only safe for idempotent requests (or conditionally idempotent ones with preconditions).

## Cloud Shell and Cloud Workstations

[Cloud Shell](https://cloud.google.com/shell/docs/how-cloud-shell-works) provisions a Debian-based Compute Engine VM (owned by Google, not shown in your projects) per user per session. It prompts you to authorize on first use, and comes with the Google Cloud CLI, Docker, Git, Helm, Gradle, Maven, npm, pip, and several language runtimes. Key numbers:

- **5 GB persistent `$HOME`**, per user and shared across projects. Software installed outside `$HOME` is lost when the VM is discarded.
- **Session ends after an hour of inactivity**; `$HOME` is deleted if you do not access Cloud Shell for 120 days.
- Per the [limitations page](https://cloud.google.com/shell/docs/limitations): default **weekly quota of 50 hours**, sessions capped at **12 hours**, and non-interactive sessions end automatically after 40 minutes. Cloud Shell is for interactive use.
- **Ephemeral mode** gives faster startup but no persistent disk.
- The container image is updated weekly, so the tools are current.

Google's Terraform documentation notes Cloud Shell is preinstalled with Terraform, and Cloud Code is available inside Cloud Shell. Pick Cloud Shell for zero-setup, ad hoc work.

When Cloud Shell's limits bite (no quota ceiling wanted, more storage, VPC placement, standardized images), move to [Cloud Workstations](https://cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/overview): managed development environments defined by **workstation configurations** (VM type, persistent storage, container image, IDE) inside **workstation clusters** attached to your VPC. They run on Compute Engine VMs in your project with a persistent disk, are reachable via browser IDE, VS Code, JetBrains, or SSH, and are governed by IAM. Google itself recommends Cloud Workstations if you need more than Cloud Shell's weekly quota.

## Cloud Code and Gemini Code Assist

[Cloud Code](https://cloud.google.com/code/docs) is the IDE tooling for Kubernetes and Cloud Run development, available in **VS Code, IntelliJ, and Cloud Shell**. It offers run-ready sample apps, Skaffold configuration editing, advanced Kubernetes YAML support, resource inspection, cluster creation in GKE, log streaming, Cloud Run support, Cloud Build support for running apps, a client library manager, Secret Manager support, Cloud Storage browsing, migration of apps to containers, and Apigee API development. It also ships with the **Gemini Code Assist** extension for in-editor code help, which is different from Gemini Cloud Assist below. Choose Cloud Code when the requirement is "IDE integration with Skaffold-based local-to-cloud iteration and inline Google Cloud API support."

## Local emulators

Emulators let teams run fast, free integration tests with no cloud project and no cost. The pattern is the same for each: start the emulator, then point the client library at it with an environment variable.

| Service | Start | Client library variable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pub/Sub | `gcloud beta emulators pubsub start --project=ID` | `PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST` | Default port 8085; state lives for the emulator session |
| Firestore | gcloud CLI | `FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST` | In-memory; data not kept across runs |
| Bigtable | gcloud CLI | `BIGTABLE_EMULATOR_HOST` | In-memory; no admin APIs to manage instances and clusters |
| Spanner | gcloud CLI | `SPANNER_EMULATOR_HOST` | Documented default `localhost:9010`; no TLS, authentication, IAM, permissions, or roles |
| Datastore | `gcloud beta emulators datastore start` | `DATASTORE_EMULATOR_HOST` | Stores to a local file by default; `--no-store-on-disk` disables it |

Sources: the [Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator), [Firestore emulator](https://cloud.google.com/firestore/docs/emulator), [Bigtable emulator](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/emulator), and [Spanner emulator](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/emulator) pages. `gcloud beta emulators pubsub env-init` prints the variables to export. Because ports can change when you restart the emulator, you must set the variables each time. The Pub/Sub emulator itself warns its "implementation may be incomplete or differ from the real system." The Spanner emulator documentation lists IAM among unsupported features, so the practical rule is: **emulators validate functional behavior, not permissions, quotas, or durability.** Test IAM and persistence in a real, isolated project. Emulators never write to the cloud backend.

## Authentication: Application Default Credentials

Authentication questions are the most common in this sub-objective. [ADC](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials) is a strategy the authentication libraries use to find credentials automatically, so the same code runs locally and in production. The search order is:

1. The `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` environment variable (a credential file).
2. The file created by `gcloud auth application-default login`.
3. The **attached service account**, returned by the metadata server.

The order does not indicate preference. Google states service account keys "create a security risk and are not recommended," because unlike other credential types a stolen key works without further information. The [setup guide](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/best-practices-applications) says ADC setup depends on where the code runs: locally, use your user credentials or **service account impersonation** through the gcloud CLI; on a resource with an attached service account (Compute Engine, Cloud Run, and so on), attach a user-managed service account; in containers on GKE, use Workload Identity Federation for GKE; elsewhere, use Workload Identity Federation. Note that `gcloud auth application-default login` supplies credentials to client libraries; the gcloud CLI itself does not use ADC and has its own credentials.

### GKE: Workload Identity Federation for GKE

[Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity) is, in most cases, the recommended way for GKE workloads to access Google Cloud services without key files. Enabling it creates a fixed workload identity pool `PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog` and deploys the GKE metadata server on each node, which intercepts ADC's token request and exchanges the pod's Kubernetes ServiceAccount token (through Security Token Service) for a short-lived federated token. Enabling it grants nothing by itself; you create IAM allow policies granting roles to a principal such as `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/SERVICEACCOUNT` (all pods using one Kubernetes ServiceAccount). Where a target service has limitations with federated tokens, link the Kubernetes ServiceAccount to an IAM service account and use impersonation instead. Either way, grant only the narrow roles needed (for BigQuery, for example, data access plus job-creation roles rather than Owner), and never mount a key as a Secret or use the Compute Engine default service account.

## Client libraries

[Cloud Client Libraries](https://cloud.google.com/apis/docs/client-libraries-explained) are the recommended way to call Cloud APIs. They provide idiomatic code per language, a consistent style across services, handle low-level communication details including authentication, install with standard package managers (npm, pip), and sometimes gain performance from gRPC. If a Cloud Client Library does not cover a service in your language, fall back to the Google API Client Library; use raw REST only when neither fits. Raw REST is still possible, but the client library significantly reduces the code you write, especially for [authentication](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/client-libraries): when you create a client, the library checks ADC automatically and manages tokens. A library only changes how you call the API; IAM is still enforced on every request.

## Gemini Cloud Assist

[Gemini Cloud Assist](https://cloud.google.com/cloud-assist/overview) is an AI collaborator embedded in the Google Cloud console that helps design, deploy, troubleshoot, and optimize workloads. It uses context such as your project and organization IDs and the console page you are viewing. Its **investigations** feature diagnoses issues from logs, errors, or natural-language prompts, ingesting logs, metrics, and configurations to explore hypotheses and trace root causes; for Cloud Run it can follow infrastructure signals down to application code. The overview page carries Preview terms, and Google warns the output can be plausible but wrong, so validate it. Do not confuse it with **Gemini Code Assist**, which helps write code in the IDE. A standalone chatbot with no resource context, or log-based metrics alone, is not the answer to "AI help aware of my resources, logs, and metrics."

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Downloading service account keys** and setting `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` on VMs or in Kubernetes Secrets. Attach an identity or use Workload Identity Federation for GKE.
- **Granting the Compute Engine default service account Owner or Editor** so "anything works." It breaks least privilege and per-workload identity.
- **Pasting `gcloud auth print-access-token` output into environment variables.** Tokens expire, leak into history, and bypass ADC.
- **Embedding OAuth client secrets with an interactive consent flow in a server app.** User OAuth flows are for accessing end-user data.
- **Writing new automation with `gsutil`** or `gsutil` without `-m` for bulk copies. Use `gcloud storage`.
- **Using emulators to validate IAM, quotas, or persistence.** They do not enforce IAM and keep data locally.
- **Treating Cloud Shell as a build server.** It is interactive, quota-limited, and sessions end.
- **Hand-rolling REST calls and retry loops** where a Cloud Client Library exists.
- **Retrying non-idempotent calls blindly.** Retry only when the operation is safe to repeat.

## Exam tips

- **Compute Engine VM calling an API: attach a service account and use ADC.** No key file, no embedded credentials, no pasted tokens; the library reads the metadata server.
- **GKE pod calling an API: Workload Identity Federation for GKE plus a least-privilege role.** Never a key in a Secret or the default service account with Owner.
- **`gcloud storage` is the recommended Cloud Storage CLI.** `gsutil -m` still works but is legacy; `bq cp` copies tables, not objects; `bq load --autodetect` loads files into BigQuery.
- **Cloud Shell: free, browser-based, pre-authenticated, 5 GB persistent `$HOME`.** Remember the 50-hour weekly quota and move to Cloud Workstations for managed, VPC-based environments.
- **Cloud Code is the IDE plugin** for VS Code, IntelliJ, and Cloud Shell with Skaffold and Kubernetes/Cloud Run tooling; Gemini Code Assist writes code, Gemini Cloud Assist troubleshoots cloud resources.
- **Emulators are started with gcloud and selected by `*_EMULATOR_HOST` variables.** They exist for Pub/Sub, Firestore, Bigtable, Spanner, and Datastore, and they do not enforce IAM.
- **ADC search order is env var file, gcloud ADC file, then attached service account;** the order is not a recommendation, and keys are the least-preferred option.
- **Prefer client libraries to raw REST.** They handle authentication through ADC, use idiomatic types, and cut boilerplate; they never bypass IAM.

flowchart TD

  E1 -->|"Yes"| K["Credential file (key or federation config)"]
